title: Man's Search for Meaning
author: Viktor E. Frankl
tagline: A psychiatrist's account of surviving the camps, and the search for meaning at the heart of life.

superpower.name: Inner Freedom
superpower.description: You choose your attitude, whatever happens.

overview: Frankl describes his experiences as a prisoner in Nazi concentration camps and the psychological phases prisoners passed through. In the second part he outlines logotherapy, his theory that the primary human drive is the search for meaning. These modules follow the book's parts and the phases Frankl describes.

chapters.part: Part One · Experiences in a Concentration Camp
chapters.title: The First Phase: Admission
chapters.summary: Frankl describes the shock of arrival: separation, the loss of possessions and identity, and a strange 'delusion of reprieve' as prisoners hoped they'd be spared. Many people found they could endure far more than they ever imagined.
keyIdeas: Shock and loss mark the first phase.
Humans can endure more than expected.
chapters.tryThis: Reflect on a time you endured something you thought you couldn't.

quiz.question: What characterised the first phase Frankl describes?
quiz.explanation: Arrival brought shock and a delusion of reprieve.

chapters.part: Part One · Experiences in a Concentration Camp
chapters.title: The Second Phase: Life in the Camp
chapters.summary: Prisoners entered a phase of apathy as a protective shell. Yet Frankl saw that an inner life — memories of loved ones, beauty, humour and a sense of purpose — helped some endure. He concludes that one freedom cannot be taken away: the freedom to choose one's attitude in any circumstance.
keyIdeas: Love and inner life sustained people.
We can always choose our attitude.
chapters.tryThis: In a frustrating moment today, consciously choose your response.

quiz.question: What freedom does Frankl say can never be taken away?
quiz.explanation: The last human freedom is choosing one's attitude.

chapters.part: Part One · Experiences in a Concentration Camp
chapters.title: The Third Phase: After Liberation
chapters.summary: Freedom at first felt unreal; prisoners had lost the ability to feel joy and had to relearn it. Some struggled with bitterness or disillusionment. Frankl notes that those who had a reason to live — a person or a task waiting for them — were better able to survive and rebuild.
keyIdeas: A reason to live aids survival.
chapters.tryThis: Write down who or what is 'waiting' for you — a reason to keep going.

quiz.question: What helped survivors most, according to Frankl?
quiz.explanation: A 'why' helps people bear almost any 'how'.

chapters.part: Part Two · Logotherapy in a Nutshell
chapters.title: The Will to Meaning
chapters.summary: Logotherapy holds that the primary human motivation is to find meaning in life — not pleasure or power. When this search is frustrated, people experience an 'existential vacuum' of emptiness and boredom. Meaning is discovered in the world, not invented inside the self.
keyIdeas: Lack of meaning creates an existential vacuum.
chapters.tryThis: Ask yourself: what does life expect from me right now?

quiz.question: What is the primary human motivation in logotherapy?
quiz.explanation: The will to meaning comes first.

chapters.part: Part Two · Logotherapy in a Nutshell
chapters.title: Three Ways to Find Meaning
chapters.summary: Frankl describes three sources of meaning: creating a work or doing a deed; experiencing something or encountering someone (especially love); and the attitude we take toward unavoidable suffering. When suffering can't be changed, we can still find meaning in how we bear it.
keyIdeas: Meaning through our attitude to suffering.
chapters.tryThis: Identify one source of meaning in each of the three areas in your life.

quiz.question: Which is one of Frankl's three sources of meaning?
quiz.explanation: Suffering can become meaningful through our response.

chapters.title: The Case for a Tragic Optimism
chapters.summary: Frankl argues we can remain optimistic despite the 'tragic triad' of pain, guilt and death: turning suffering into achievement, guilt into a chance to change for the better, and life's transitoriness into an incentive to act responsibly.
keyIdeas: Optimism despite pain, guilt and death.
chapters.tryThis: Pick one regret and decide how it can push you to act better.

quiz.question: What is the 'tragic triad'?
quiz.explanation: Frankl's three inescapable facts of life.
